## `stabilis.gui`

A local page for the routine work, so it needs no CLI flags.

    stabilis gui                    # opens http://127.0.0.1:8765
    stabilis gui --root ~/data      # confine the file browser

**This is a client of the library, not part of it.** Everything under
`gui/` imports from `stabilis` and nothing in `stabilis` imports from
`gui/`, so the whole package could be lifted out and shipped separately
without the engine noticing. That direction is deliberate and load-bearing:
the API is not permitted to grow a shape because a page found it
convenient, and the page is free to be rewritten because no answer depends
on it.

**It computes nothing a user would quote.** It reads files, builds derived
columns, chooses which stretches of a record to keep, and draws pictures.
Every variance, every degree of freedom and every confidence bound comes
from `stats/`, through the same calls the CLI makes, so the page and the
command line cannot disagree.

The work is arranged as four stages, which is the order the questions
actually arrive in:

1. **Data** -- pick a file, confirm what its columns are called, look at
   them, and mark the stretches worth analysing. Nothing is converted or
   assumed here; the point is to see the record before deciding anything.
2. **Prepare** -- say what the numbers *are*: phase or frequency, in which
   units, at what rate, and what arithmetic turns the file's columns into
   the quantity of interest.
3. **Analyse** -- run an estimator over what stage 2 produced, and read the
   result off an interactive curve with the table and the equivalent script
   beside it.
4. **Bench** -- describe the setup instead of the file: which oscillators,
   which instruments and channels, and which measurement is which pair.
   Says whether the setup can separate its clocks at all *before* any data
   is read, then assigns each measurement a file and a column and solves
   the N-cornered hat.

Stage 4 is the only one that looks at several files at once, and it is the
one that must assume least about them. Stages 1-3 examine a file the user
just chose and is already looking at; a bench is six exports from six
instruments, each with its own delimiter, timebase, dropouts and glitch.
So the delimiter, the units, the timebase, the kept stretches and the
outlier threshold are all *per measurement*, the record is drawn before it
is solved, and what each file needed tolerating is reported against the row
it belongs to rather than once for the bench.

Stage 4 is the one place the page touches `stabilis.bench`, and it does so
as a client like everything else here: it strips each measurement to its
column itself and hands `bench.solve` a mapping of finished results, which
is all that function has ever wanted. See `bench.py`.

Modules: `files` reaches the disk and caches what it read, `expr` parses
column arithmetic without an evaluator, `prepare` turns columns into series
the library accepts, `request` reads the settings every endpoint is sent,
`api` serves the reading and drawing endpoints, `analysis` is the one that
runs an estimator, `bench` is the setup stage and `benchdata` the half of it
that reaches a file, `server` is the HTTP and the bind, and `assets/` is the
page itself.

Re-exports: `serve`, `DEFAULT_PORT`, `estimators`, `Handler`, `PHASE_UNITS`, `FREQ_UNITS`, `safe_path`, `cache_clear`.

## `stabilis.gui.analysis`

`POST /api/analyze` -- the only endpoint that runs an estimator.

Split out of `api.py` because it is the half with a different job. The rest
of the page reads files and reduces arrays for drawing; this takes a series
the library will accept, hands it to `stats/`, and flattens what comes back
into parallel arrays the canvas can plot.

**Nothing here computes a statistic.** Every variance, degree of freedom and
confidence bound comes from the library, through the same calls `cli/`
makes, which is what stops the page and the command line from being able to
disagree about a number. There is a test that runs the recipe this module
prints, by hand, and demands identical output.

#### `analyze`

```python
analyze(root, req: dict) -> dict
```

Run one estimator over every selected stretch of every series.

Each window becomes its own curve unless `join` is set, in which case the
stretches between windows become gaps in one longer record. Both are
honest; neither invents a sample. See `prepare.exclude_between`.

## `stabilis.gui.api`

The page's endpoints. Everything numeric, nothing rendered.

The old page sent pictures: matplotlib drew a PNG on the server and the
browser displayed it, so every zoom, every drag and every relabelling was a
round trip through a figure. This one sends **numbers** -- a min/max
envelope for the raw view, a table of tau and sigma for the result -- and
the browser draws them on a canvas. That is what makes panning and zooming
free, and it takes matplotlib out of the GUI's dependencies entirely, so
`stabilis gui` is now as numpy-only as the core.

The split across the endpoints follows what actually costs time:

* `capabilities` asks the library what it can do, so the page holds no
  second copy of the estimator list to fall behind it.
* `open` reads the file, once, and answers everything about its shape. It
  is the only slow call.
* `traces` slices and decimates what is already in memory. This is the one
  the page fires on every interaction, and it must stay in milliseconds.
* `analyze` -- in `analysis.py` -- is the only one that runs an estimator.

**No endpoint computes a statistic itself.** `traces` reduces points for
drawing and says so; every number a user could quote comes from `stats/`.

#### `estimators`

```python
estimators() -> tuple[str, ...]
```

Every estimator the library has registered, in name order.

Read from the registry rather than listed here, so an estimator added to
`stats/` -- or supplied by a third party through the `stabilis.estimator`
entry point -- appears in the page without this file being touched. A
hard-coded list is how a GUI ends up quietly older than its engine: the
day this was changed the library had grown three estimators the page did
not offer, and nothing anywhere said so.

#### `capabilities`

```python
capabilities(root, query: dict) -> dict
```

What the page should offer, asked of the library rather than assumed.

The estimator list, the tau grids and the unit tables all live in the
engine. Fetching them means the page has no second copy to drift.

#### `GET_ROUTES`

```python
GET_ROUTES = {'/api/files': list_files, '/api/capabilities': capabilities}
```

#### `POST_ROUTES`

```python
POST_ROUTES = {'/api/open': open_file, '/api/traces': traces, '/api/analyze': analysis.analyze, '/api/bench/check': bench.check_bench, '/api/bench/solve': bench.solve_bench, '/api/bench/load': bench.load_bench}
```

## `stabilis.gui.bench`

The bench stage: which clock, against which, through which channel.

Stages 1-3 answer "what is this record worth". This one answers the
question a calibration lab actually starts from -- *I have four oscillators
and two counters; which of these numbers belongs to which clock?* -- and it
is the same three questions as before with the arithmetic done by
`bench/`: describe the setup, assign each measurement its data, solve.

**The library is handed results, never files.** `bench.solve` takes a
`{measurement id -> StabilityResult}` mapping and does one non-negative
least-squares solve per tau; it has no notion of columns, units or headers
and must not grow one. So the stripping is this module's job -- pick the
columns out of the file, subtract the pedestal, scale the units, crop to
the selected stretch -- and by the time anything the library owns is
called, a measurement is an array with a sample rate. That split is why
`Measurement` needs no column field: the page never asks the engine to go
looking for a column, so there is no second answer to disagree with.

The work is exactly the work `analysis.py` does for one series, done once
per measurement, through the same `expr` -> `prepare` -> registry path. The
recipe printed beside the answer is the whole thing as runnable code,
including the pedestal and the unit scaling, so the session reproduces
without the mouse.

Two names spelled `bench` meet in this file. `..bench` is the library's
measurement-setup model; this module is the page's client of it, and every
import of the former is written relatively so the two never blur.

#### `check_bench`

```python
check_bench(root, req: dict) -> dict
```

Can this setup separate its oscillators? Reads no data file.

Fired on every edit, because the answer is worth most while the
experiment is still being planned -- "go and measure B against D" is
cheap advice on a Tuesday and expensive advice after a fortnight of
logging. `root` is unused for exactly that reason and is kept only
because every route is called the same way.

#### `load_bench`

```python
load_bench(root, req: dict) -> dict
```

Read a `bench.json` from under the root, for editing in the page.

Read only. The page saves by handing the browser a download, so this
server never writes to the disk it can read -- the bind is to localhost
because a file reader is already something worth confining, and a file
writer would be a different conversation.

Hashes are checked and *reported*, never enforced: an unsolvable bench
is still one worth opening and correcting, and refusing to display it
would leave the user with a text editor and no diagnostic.

#### `solve_bench`

```python
solve_bench(root, req: dict) -> dict
```

Strip every measurement to its column, estimate, then hand it over.

Nothing here decides anything a user would quote. The estimator comes
from the registry, the solve from `bench/`, and the only arithmetic in
this function is picking the source block out of the answer.

## `stabilis.gui.benchdata`

Turning one measurement's assignment into a result the solver can take.

This is the half of stage 4 that reaches a file. `bench.py` orchestrates --
check the graph, gather the rows, hand them over -- and everything between
"the user pointed at a column" and "here is a `StabilityResult`" happens
here, once per measurement.

Split out of `bench.py` for the same reason `analysis.py` is split out of
`api.py`: it is the half with a different job, and a different set of ways
to be wrong. The orchestration is about a graph; this is about somebody
else's counter output.

**It assumes nothing about the data.** Six measurements from six
instruments are six formats, six delimiters, six timebases and six
different kinds of mess, so every one of those is a per-measurement
setting rather than a property of the bench. What a file needed tolerating
to be read at all, how many points were gaps, how many an outlier
threshold removed, and how far the timetags wander from a clean grid are
all reported per row -- "something was tolerated somewhere" is not
actionable when the something belongs to one of six counters.

#### `rate_notes`

```python
rate_notes(prepared: list) -> list[str]
```

Say when the counters disagree, before the tau grids fail to meet.

Different instruments run at different rates, which is normal and fine
-- but `bench.solve` intersects tau grids and interpolates nothing, so
rates that are not related by a power of two share very few taus and
may share none. When that happens the failure arrives from
`_common_taus` as "the measurements share no averaging time", which is
accurate and says nothing about which row is the odd one out. This
names them while the numbers are still on screen.

A timebase read off timetags also has scatter, and a counter dropping
the occasional point shows up here as jitter long before it shows up in
a deviation.

#### `explain_failure`

```python
explain_failure(exc: ValueError, prepared: list) -> ValueError
```

Add what the page knows to what the solver said.

`bench.solve` refuses records that share no averaging time. That is the
right refusal -- nothing here interpolates onto a common grid -- and it
names the spans, but it cannot say why two counters that both ran at
1 Hz ended up on different grids. The page can: it knows each row's rate
and whether that rate was given or read off a timetag column.

The usual culprit is float64, and an MJD column is the standard way to
meet it. Day number 59000 has a float64 spacing of 7.3e-12 d = 6.3e-7 s,
so a one-second step is resolved to about 2e-7 relative; `af/rate` then
misses an exact 1.000 s by far more than the nanosecond tolerance the
intersection allows. **The record is fine. The timebase is quantized.**
An explicit rate fixes it, and saying so is worth more than repeating
that the spans do not meet.

Returns the exception to raise rather than raising, so the caller keeps
the `raise ... from` chain and unrelated failures pass through
untouched.

#### `measure`

```python
measure(root, measurement, spec: dict, name: str, taus, max_af)
```

One measurement, from file to `StabilityResult`.

**The bench is authoritative about what the quantity is.** Phase or
frequency comes from `Measurement.kind` and the sample interval from
`Measurement.tau0_s` when it is set, not from anything typed on this
screen -- those two facts belong to the experiment, they are what
`bench.json` carries to the CLI, and letting a control here contradict
them is precisely how the page and `stabilis bench solve` would come to
disagree about one file. The unit, the column expression and the crop
describe the *file*, which the bench says nothing about, so those are
the page's to supply.

#### `preamble`

```python
preamble() -> list[str]
```

Import lines and setup shared by every generated bench script.

#### `recipe`

```python
recipe(measurement, spec, table, labels, text, is_phase, factor, rate)
```

The exact calls that rebuild this measurement's series.

`read_table` rather than the friendlier `load_phase(column=...)` even
when the expression is a single column, and the reason is the pedestal.
`prepare.build_series` subtracts the first finite sample before scaling
the units -- which is what buys back the float64 resolution a 0.35 s
phase offset would otherwise spend -- and `load_phase` does not. The
shorter recipe would therefore reproduce the answer without reproducing
the arithmetic, and a recipe that is only nearly what happened is worth
less than no recipe at all.

## `stabilis.gui.expr`

Column arithmetic for the page, without an evaluator behind the box.

`edit.parse_expression` in the library covers a *sum of whole columns* --
`NCS - VSL`, `-VSL` -- and stops there deliberately. The page needs a
little more than that: a channel scaled into different units, a divider
ratio backed out, a mean removed. So this module implements exactly that
little more, and nothing else.

**There is still no Python evaluator anywhere near a user string.** This is
a hand-written tokenizer and recursive-descent parser over a closed grammar
-- numbers, column references, `+ - * /`, parentheses, unary sign. There is
no name lookup that can reach a builtin, no attribute access, no call
syntax, no indexing, no comprehension. An input the grammar does not
describe is refused with a message, never passed on to something that might
run it. The same reasoning is why this library refuses pickle: a file, or
an expression, arriving from someone else's rig is untrusted input.

Two rules that matter to the answer rather than to safety:

**Column names win over numbers.** A label is matched before a numeric
literal is tried, longest first, so a file whose header really is `2` still
works and a label containing a space or a minus sign is usable. Where the
label form is not wanted, `#2` always means the third column by position.

**An expression that names no column is refused.** `2 - 1` reads as
arithmetic here, not as "column 2 minus column 1" the way it does in
`edit.parse_expression`. Silently returning the scalar 1.0 would be a wrong
answer that looks plausible, so the parser insists that at least one column
took part and names the `#N` syntax in the error.

#### `ExpressionError`

```python
class ExpressionError
```

The expression is not in the grammar, or names something absent.

#### `tokenize`

```python
tokenize(expression: str, labels) -> list[tuple[str, object]]
```

`"NCS - VSL/2"` into `[("col", 1), ("op", "-"), ...]`.

Longest label first, so `VSL_B` is not read as `VSL` followed by
rubbish. Matching is case-sensitive first and case-insensitive second,
because a header is a name and typing it in the wrong case is a typo
rather than a different column.

#### `evaluate`

```python
evaluate(expression: str, labels, rows) -> tuple[np.ndarray, int]
```

The column `expression` describes, and how many divisions blew up.

`rows` is 2-D, one column per label. Returns `(values, n_infinite)`.

A NaN anywhere in a term makes the result NaN there, which is what
should happen -- a difference is unknown wherever either side is. That
needs no counting, because those points are already gaps and the record
summary reports them.

An **infinity** is different: it means a divisor was exactly zero, and
it is a fact about the arithmetic rather than about the input. It
becomes a gap, because NaN is this library's gap representation and
every estimator already knows what to do with one, and the count comes
back so the page can say it happened instead of it being absorbed
silently.

## `stabilis.gui.files`

Reaching files, and holding one in memory once it has been read.

Two jobs that both exist for speed or for safety, and nothing else.

**`_safe` is the whole security model.** The page reads files from the
machine it runs on, so every path from the browser goes through it. It
resolves `..` *before* the check, so a path that climbs out of the root is
refused rather than quietly rebased onto it -- the difference between
saying no and serving the wrong file.

**The table cache is what makes the page reactive.** Every interaction --
retyping a label, dragging a range, switching units -- used to re-read the
whole file, which on a 200 MB export is seconds of wall clock for a change
that touched no bytes on disk. Reading once and keying on
`(path, mtime_ns, size)` turns all of those into an array slice. The key
includes mtime and size rather than a hash because rehashing 200 MB to
decide whether to reuse it would cost more than the read it saves, and a
file that changed underneath us changes at least one of the two in every
case that is not a deliberate forgery.

#### `DATA_SUFFIXES`

```python
DATA_SUFFIXES = ('.dat', '.txt', '.csv', '.tsv', '.phase', '.freq', '')
```

Extensions offered in the file browser. Not a security control -- `safe_path` is -- just a way to keep the listing readable in a directory full of unrelated files.

#### `Table`

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Table
```

One file, read whole, with everything the page asks about it.

`rows` is 2-D and read-only. It is handed to several requests at once
-- `ThreadingHTTPServer` serves the page's parallel fetches on separate
threads -- so making it immutable is what stops one request's editing
from being another's input.

*Fields*

```python
path: str
labels: tuple[str, ...]
rows: np.ndarray
defects: str
has_header: bool
n: int
n_columns: int
header_row_dropped: bool = False
```

#### `safe_path`

```python
safe_path(root: Path, candidate: str) -> Path
```

Resolve `candidate` under `root`, or refuse.

#### `listing`

```python
listing(root: Path, rel: str) -> dict
```

Directories and plausible data files at `rel`, for the picker.

#### `load_table`

```python
load_table(path: Path, delimiter: str | None=None) -> Table
```

The file as columns, from cache when it has not changed on disk.

#### `cache_bytes`

```python
cache_bytes() -> int
```

Bytes currently held. For the tests, and for answering "why is this big".

#### `cache_clear`

```python
cache_clear() -> None
```

Drop everything held. For tests, and for `--no-cache` reasoning.

#### `column_facts`

```python
column_facts(table: Table) -> list[dict]
```

Per column: how much of it is real, its span, and whether it ticks.

The monotonic flag is what lets the page offer a time column instead of
making the user find it. Computed on the first 4096 rows: a timebase
that starts by increasing and stops later is a broken timebase, and the
page says so when the column is actually selected rather than scanning
two million rows to decorate a dropdown.

#### `timebase`

```python
timebase(table: Table, index: int, fmt: str | None)
```

`(rate_hz, jitter, note)` from a time column, numeric or text.

The numeric column goes through `parse_times` rather than straight to
`infer_rate`, even though it is already an array of floats and the
shortcut is tempting. **A timestamp is not a number of seconds until
something says which epoch it counts from.** An MJD column ticks by
1/86400 per sample at 1 Hz, so handing it to `infer_rate` unconverted
returns 86400 Hz and every tau in the report is wrong by that factor,
plausibly and silently. `parse_times` classifies by the range the values
actually occupy, converts, and refuses with `AmbiguousTimebase` when the
evidence fits more than one format -- at which point the page's "time
format" control is the answer, and guessing would not have been.

Non-finite entries are dropped first: a gap in the timestamps is skipped
rather than interpolated, which is what `infer_rate` documents.

A column of ISO timestamps is entirely non-numeric, so `read_table`
holds NaN for it and the text has to be re-read from disk. That costs a
second pass over the file and happens only when such a column is chosen.

## `stabilis.gui.prepare`

Turning a file's columns into series the library will accept.

Everything between "the user has picked a file" and "an estimator can run"
lives here: which stretches of the record to keep, what the numbers in it
are in, and how to draw two million points into a few hundred pixels
without lying about them.

**Nothing here estimates anything.** The page's whole job is to hand the
library good input; the moment a variance is wanted, `stats/` computes it.
That boundary is why this can be rewritten freely without any risk to an
answer.

#### `PHASE_UNITS`

```python
PHASE_UNITS = {'s': 1.0, 'ms': 0.001, 'us': 1e-06, 'ns': 1e-09, 'ps': 1e-12}
```

What the numbers in the file are in, and the factor that turns them into what the library wants. Phase is seconds; fractional frequency is dimensionless. A file in nanoseconds analysed as seconds is wrong by a billion and looks entirely plausible on a log axis, so an unrecognised unit is an error rather than a silent 1.0.

#### `FREQ_UNITS`

```python
FREQ_UNITS = {'fractional': 1.0, 'ppm': 1e-06, 'ppb': 1e-09, 'ppt': 1e-15}
```

#### `PREVIEW_POINTS`

```python
PREVIEW_POINTS = 1400
```

A trace is a picture, and a picture has a few hundred pixel columns.

#### `unit_factor`

```python
unit_factor(unit, is_phase: bool) -> float
```

The multiplier into the library's units, refusing anything unknown.

#### `envelope`

```python
envelope(values: np.ndarray, start: int, stop: int, target: int=PREVIEW_POINTS) -> dict
```

The `[start, stop)` slice reduced to one min/max pair per pixel column.

**Not stride sampling.** Taking every k-th point would hide exactly the
outliers this view exists to find -- a one-sample glitch has a (k-1)/k
chance of vanishing, better than 99% at the reduction used on a large
record. Keeping each bucket's minimum and maximum preserves the visual
envelope, so a spike is still a spike and a range dragged over it means
what it looks like it means.

Vectorized through `reduceat` rather than a Python loop over buckets:
this runs on every drag, every zoom and every keystroke that changes an
expression, and a loop over a thousand buckets is the difference between
a page that feels live and one that stutters. `fmin`/`fmax` skip NaN, so
a bucket holding one good sample among gaps still reports it, while a
bucket that is entirely gap correctly comes back NaN and breaks the line.

Returns bucket start indices with `lo`/`hi`, or plain samples when the
slice is already short enough to draw honestly point for point.

#### `clamp_windows`

```python
clamp_windows(windows, size: int) -> list[tuple[int, int]]
```

The page's `[start, stop]` pairs as real, ordered, merged indices.

Overlapping windows are merged rather than kept apart, because two
overlapping selections of the same record are one selection -- leaving
them separate would analyse the shared stretch twice and quietly
double-count it in anything that later averaged the results.

#### `build_series`

```python
build_series(values: np.ndarray, rate_hz: float, is_phase: bool, factor: float)
```

A `PhaseSeries` or `FreqSeries` from raw column values.

Built at full length and cropped afterwards through `edit.select_range`,
rather than sliced here and constructed short. The library call is what
writes the selection into the step log, and a range that reached the
answer without appearing in provenance is exactly the undocumented
exclusion this project exists to make impossible.

The constant pedestal is removed **before** the unit conversion, not
after, and the order is load-bearing. These columns routinely carry one
-- 0.35 s in the record this was built against, where float64 spacing is
5.5e-17 s and the fluctuations live below it. Every estimator here
differences the phase, so subtracting a constant changes no answer and
buys back the resolution `types.precision_ratio` would otherwise be
warning about.

Scaling first would spend that resolution before reclaiming it.
`x * 1e-12` rounds each element independently to within half an ulp,
which on a 0.35 pedestal is a perturbation of about 4e-17 s scattered
across a signal of about 1e-12 s -- and it does not cancel in the
subtraction that follows, because each element rounded its own way. The
measured cost was a deviation that moved in the sixth figure depending
on which unit the same file was read in. Subtracting first leaves the
multiply acting on numbers whose magnitude is already the signal's, and
the units then scale the answer exactly.

#### `exclude_between`

```python
exclude_between(series, spans, reason: str)
```

Mark everything outside `spans` as a gap, and record that it happened.

This is the `join=True` reading of several selected windows: one record
from the first window's start to the last one's end, with the stretches
nobody selected turned into gaps for the estimators' documented gap
policy to handle.

**Nothing is filled in.** Interpolating across an excluded stretch would
invent the data whose exclusion was the entire point, and there is no
imputer in the library to borrow -- gap filling is a later milestone,
validated against records where the removed points are known. The
alternative reading, one independent result per window, needs no
masking at all and is what the page does by default.

Written here rather than in `edit.py` because it is a consequence of a
multi-window gesture, which is a page idea; the step still goes through
`log.record`, so the provenance is the same shape as any library edit.

#### `crop`

```python
crop(series, lo: int, hi: int, reason: str, lines: list)
```

`edit.select_range` when it would change anything, echoed either way.

#### `reject_outliers`

```python
reject_outliers(series, threshold, reason: str, lines: list)
```

`edit.drop_outliers` if a threshold was given, echoed if it ran.

---

## `stabilis.gui.request`

Reading a request from the page: what file, which columns, at what rate.

Every endpoint is handed the same JSON object and has to answer the same few
questions of it. They live here rather than in `api.py` so that `analysis.py`
can ask them too without the two importing each other.

Nothing here touches the numbers. It resolves a path, names some columns and
settles a sample rate; what those columns then mean is `prepare`'s job and
what they are worth is `stats/`'s.

#### `floats`

```python
floats(a) -> list
```

A float array as JSON, with every non-finite value as `null`.

`json.dumps` writes a bare `NaN`, which `JSON.parse` refuses outright --
so a gapped column would take the whole page down rather than showing a
break in the line. `null` is both valid JSON and what the canvas plotter
already treats as "lift the pen", which is what a gap is.

#### `table_for`

```python
table_for(root, req) -> files.Table
```

The requested file, from cache when it has not changed on disk.

#### `labels_for`

```python
labels_for(req, table) -> tuple[str, ...]
```

The column names to resolve expressions against.

The file's header if it has one, the reader's positional names if not,
and **whatever the user typed in preference to either**. A header is a
hint from whoever wrote the logger, not an authority: `ch1` and `ch2`
are legal names and useless ones, and the person reading the plot is the
one who knows which is the maser. An override of the wrong length is
ignored rather than partially applied, since a shifted name list would
silently analyse the wrong column.

#### `specs`

```python
specs(req, table)
```

The series the page asked for: `(expression, label, windows)`.

Windows are a property of the *record*, not of one column: they are
chosen by dragging on a shared sample axis, and every column of an export
is on that same timebase. So the request-level `windows` applies to all
of them, and a series may still carry its own list to override it --
which is what a caller driving this endpoint from a script would want,
even though the page has no control that does it.

#### `rate_for`

```python
rate_for(req, table)
```

`(rate_hz, jitter, note)` -- given by the user, or read off a timebase.

An explicit rate always wins. A rate inferred from timetags is a
measurement with its own scatter, and the page shows that scatter, but a
user who knows their counter runs at exactly 1 Hz should not have to
argue with a median.

---

## `stabilis.gui.server`

The HTTP layer: routing, static assets, and the bind.

**It binds to 127.0.0.1 and nothing else.** The page reads files from the
machine it runs on, so a wider bind would be handing a stranger a file
reader. `--root` narrows it further, to one directory tree, and paths that
try to escape that root are refused rather than normalized into it.

**Why a browser page rather than a desktop toolkit.** tkinter is not in this
environment's Python (Debian splits it into `python3-tk`, which needs root),
and PySide is a hundred-megabyte download to draw a form. `http.server` is
in the standard library, every machine already has a browser, and it works
the same from WSL, Linux and Windows.

The page's own files live in `assets/` and are served from disk rather than
embedded in a Python string. The old version kept the whole page in one raw
literal, which meant a `\n` written for JavaScript had to survive Python's
escaping to reach the browser as two characters -- it did not, once, and the
symptom was a page that rendered blank with nothing saying why. Files on
disk cannot have that failure, and they let the Content-Security-Policy drop
`unsafe-inline` for both scripts and styles.

#### `DEFAULT_PORT`

```python
DEFAULT_PORT = 8765
```

#### `Handler`

```python
class Handler
```

Routes to `api`, serves `assets/`, and turns exceptions into messages.

*method* `log_message(self, *args) -> None`

Silence per-request logging; the console is for real messages.

*method* `do_GET(self) -> None`

*method* `do_POST(self) -> None`

#### `serve`

```python
serve(port: int=DEFAULT_PORT, root: Path | None=None, open_browser: bool=True) -> None
```

Run the local page until interrupted.
